title: From Chennai Handlooms to Dior Runways: How Madras Checks Conquered Global Fashion
excerpt: The checked cotton fabric born on India's Coromandel coast has travelled through colonial trade, Ivy League wardrobes and high fashion — and is now finding its way home.
body:
• Madras checks, the distinctive cotton plaid fabric from Chennai's Coromandel coast, has been adopted by global fashion houses including Dior, Burberry and Brooks Brothers over the past century.
  • Indian designers and manufacturers are now reclaiming the textile, with initiatives like Original Madras Trading Company reviving authentic handloom production in Chennai.
  • India's handloom sector has shrunk from 6.5 million weavers in the mid-1990s to about 3.5 million today, accounting for just 15% of total cloth production.
  • Calls are growing for geographical indication recognition to protect the authentic fabric and create better economic value for weaving communities.

A Fabric With a Global Passport

The story of Madras checks begins not in a fashion studio but on the Coromandel coast. The distinctive plaid cotton takes its name from the port city of Madras — now Chennai — from where it was historically exported, though the fabric itself was woven across several centres along the southeastern Indian coastline. From there, it moved outward along maritime trade routes that carried spices, cotton and dyes across the Indian Ocean and beyond, according to The Hindu.

In Nigeria, particularly among the Igbo and Kalabari communities, brightly coloured Madras cotton became known as George cloth or Injiri, worn during ceremonial occasions. The handwoven checks — often in vivid combinations of red, indigo, yellow and green — were labelled "Real Madras" to distinguish them from machine-made European imitations.

By the early 20th century, the fabric had quietly entered American fashion. Wealthy Americans returning from winter holidays in the Bahamas brought the colourful shirts back with them, and by the 1950s, Madras had settled into the wardrobes of Ivy League campuses as shorthand for relaxed summer dressing.

Revival on Home Ground

For Ranvir Shah of the Chennai-based Original Madras Trading Company, the revival is personal. His family has worked with the fabric for over 50 years, initially exporting garments to American labels.

"At some point, it struck me that we were being garment coolies. We needed to create something of our own," Ranvir told The Hindu. The initiative began with just two handlooms in Chennai, reviving traditional practices that had declined as machine-made imitations spread globally.

Ranvir is now exploring an idea that could give the fabric even deeper cultural identity: family-specific Madras checks that could be passed down through generations, much like Scotland's clan tartans, which are officially recorded in the Scottish Register of Tartans.

In Puducherry, the label Wunderhaus Handmade is transforming traditional checks into contemporary windcheaters, shacket shirts and trousers. "We're witnessing a resurgence in their popularity," says founder Kedar Maddula.

The Challenge Ahead

Renewed visibility has not necessarily translated into economic stability for the weaving communities that produce the fabric. Research based on the Fourth All India Handloom Census shows the sector currently supports about 3.5 million workers, down from roughly 6.5 million in the mid-1990s. Handlooms today account for only about 15% of India's total cloth production.

"The tension between handloom and powerloom has always shaped textiles like Madras checks," says Mumbai-based textile professional Siddhant Beriwal. "Powerloom fabrics can replicate the visual look at a fraction of the cost."

Beriwal suggests that geographical indication recognition and more organised export channels could create a stronger value proposition for designers, buyers and the weavers who keep the tradition alive.

Researcher Phyllida Jay frames the stakes plainly: "True innovation occurs when a craft remains true to its roots yet alive to possibilities." After decades of being exported, imitated and overlooked at home, Madras checks appears to be finding its way back — not as a trend, but as a textile with history, identity and a second act.
